input: This review examines the cost of the regional delivery route, drawing on carrier invoices for the last 12 months as its evidence base. The route is not a short one: each trip covers 755 km, and the carrier charges $1.45 per km, so the cost of a single trip is already considerable before any question of frequency is even considered. Frequency, however, is very much part of the picture, because the route runs 327 trips per year, and once that frequency is taken into account the annual transport cost builds up to $358k, which is a substantial commitment within the wider distribution budget. It is important to note that the trip count should not be understood as counting only those journeys in which the vehicle is carrying goods for delivery: empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the return legs and other unloaded movements are fully reflected in the figure as well. It is also worth emphasising that the annual figure has not been assembled from estimates or from standard rates applied in the abstract; it is grounded in what was actually charged, as recorded on carrier invoices for the last 12 months. In overall terms, therefore, the annual transport cost of $358k for the regional delivery route, arising from 755 km per trip at $1.45 per km over 327 trips per year with empty running included in the count, represents the complete invoiced cost of running the route over the period, and it forms the baseline against which the cost of any alternative arrangement would have to be measured.
target:
The regional delivery route costs $358k per year. The evidence base is carrier invoices for the last 12 months, and the cost is stated on that basis. Each trip covers 755 km at $1.45 per km, and the route runs 327 trips per year. Empty running is included in the trip count, so the annual figure covers loaded and empty legs together.

Two quantities set the cost. Distance and rate fix the charge per trip, because 755 km at $1.45 per km is billed on every trip whether the vehicle carries a load or returns empty. Trip count then scales the per-trip charge to the year. A rate change and a trip-count change are different levers: a lower rate reduces the cost of every kilometre on every trip, while fewer trips remove whole trips at the full per-trip charge, and neither saving implies the other. Service level enters through the same count, since a route that must run whether or not a full load is ready commits the empty legs that the count includes.

Comparisons with later periods hold only on the same basis. The $358k total rests on carrier invoices for the last 12 months, with 327 trips per year and empty running inside the count. A later invoice total stated on a different trip definition, or with empty running stripped out, would differ from the present figure even if rates and distances had not moved, and the difference would be an artefact of the basis rather than a change in the cost of the route itself. Route planning reads the figure the same way. Consolidating deliveries acts on trip count, renegotiating the carrier contract acts on the rate, and backloading acts on the empty share inside the count that is already charged.
